name.en-US: The Seven Brothers and St. Felicitas
name.pt-BR: Os Sete Irmãos e Santa Felicidade

prayerExcerpt.en-US: Let them imitate the earnestness of St. Felicitas in forming to perfect virtue the tender souls which God hath committed to their charge.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Imitem eles o empenho de Santa Felicidade em formar para a perfeita virtude as tenras almas que Deus confiou aos seus cuidados.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-10-the-seven-brothers.md Reflection, second sentence, its first clause (before ", and with this Saint"), closed with a full stop (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Felicitas and her seven sons, grouped half-length inside the arched window: Felicitas in the centre, a little taller than the rest, a noble Roman widow in a deep plum-violet stola with a dark-grey palla drawn over her head as a veil, her right arm round the shoulders of her youngest son and her left hand raised toward heaven; the seven sons around her in graded heights, the three eldest standing behind at her right and left, the four younger in front, all in plain Roman tunics of white, saffron, sage-green and russet wool with short mantles, several holding green palms. Behind them, second-century Rome from the Via Salaria: umbrella pines and cypresses, a low brick tomb-chapel over a catacomb entrance, the walls and roofs of the city in warm evening light. Grave, tender and steadfast; no wounds, no instruments, no lettering. Keep all eight figures inside the arched window, eight clearly separate faces.
cards.face: Eight clearly different people of one Roman family, fair-olive skin. FELICITAS (centre), about fifty-five: a LONG face with HIGH, FLAT cheekbones and a STRONG, SQUARE, slightly prominent chin; a long, straight nose whose tip turns a little down, deep-set grey-brown eyes under thick, straight dark brows, a firm, wide mouth with fine lines at its corners; dark hair greying at the temples under the veil; her gaze lifted, fearless. The SONS: (1) JANUARIUS, the eldest, about twenty-four, behind at her right: a LONG, NARROW face, a thin, AQUILINE nose, deep-set dark eyes, a short, close black beard. (2) FELIX, about twenty-two, behind at her left: a BROAD, SQUARE face, a SHORT, BLUNT nose, wide-set brown eyes, clean-shaven, thick straight black hair. (3) PHILIP, about twenty, behind beside Felix: a HEART-SHAPED face, a fine straight nose, large dark eyes, a faint first moustache, wavy brown hair. (4) SILVANUS, about eighteen, front left: a ROUND face, a small SNUB nose, a few freckles, light-brown curls. (5) ALEXANDER, about sixteen, front: an OVAL face with his mother's long, straight nose, straight dark hair with a fringe. (6) VITALIS, about fourteen, front: a small TRIANGULAR face with a pointed chin, prominent ears, cropped black hair. (7) MARTIALIS, the youngest, about twelve, under her arm: a chubby child's face with full round cheeks and tight black curls, looking up at her.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. The book tells a noble Roman widow whose seven sons were martyred by different deaths before her eyes; the Depositio Martyrum (fourth century) already keeps the seven on 10 July in four cemeteries, and Felicitas's tomb on the Via Salaria is known. The Nuremberg Chronicle shows her veiled with her sons' heads on a sword. The faces are ours, graded by age.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Felicitas of Rome (lead: Nuremberg Chronicle woodcut)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-10-the-seven-brothers (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: Lord, Thou art able by the weakest means to humble the pride of Thy enemies.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Senhor, és capaz, pelos mais fracos meios, de humilhar a soberba dos Teus inimigos.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-11-james.md, third paragraph, the first clause of his prayer on the tower (before "; defeat these multitudes"), closed with a full stop; the chapter has no Reflection, so the card has none (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. James of Nisibis, half-length, as a fourth-century Syrian bishop who had been a mountain hermit: a coarse, dark goat-hair tunic, and over it a white wool omophorion with small dark crosses worn round the neck and falling in front; no mitre. He stands on the top of a square stone tower of the city walls of Nisibis, his right hand raised in prayer toward heaven, his left resting on the parapet. Below and far off, the Mesopotamian plain under a hot sky with the Persian camp: tents, a few small elephants and horsemen, and a faint dark haze of gnats drifting over them; behind the tower, the flat roofs and a small early church of Nisibis. Grave and prayerful, not wrathful; no battle, no lettering.
cards.face: A Syrian of Mesopotamia of about seventy, sun-darkened and weathered from years in the open air, with a SQUARE, BIG-BONED face — a HEAVY, FLAT BROW RIDGE running straight across, a BROAD, FLAT-BRIDGED nose with wide nostrils, SMALL, DEEP-SET, very dark eyes under bushy black-and-grey brows, HIGH, FLAT cheekbones, a WIDE, straight mouth; a very long, dense black beard heavily streaked with grey, falling in one mass to the chest; thick, rough grey-black hair cut short; the gaze lifted, intent.
cards.basis: No likeness survives; the Hildesheim reliquary head is an idealised medieval bust. The book and Theodoret tell a hermit of the mountains, lightly clothed, living in the open, then the bishop who prayed from the walls during Shapur II's siege. The heavy, weathered face and long beard are our reading of that Syrian ascetic.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Jacob of Nisibis (lead: Hildesheim reliquary)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-11-james (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: The heroic act which merited for St. John Gualbert his conversion was the forgiveness of his enemy.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: O ato heroico que mereceu para São João Gualberto sua conversão foi o perdão de seu inimigo.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-12-john-gualbert.md Reflection, first sentence (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. John Gualbert, half-length, as the founder-abbot of Vallombrosa: the ash-grey Benedictine habit of the early Vallombrosans with a full cowl and hood lying on the shoulders, a plain wooden abbot's staff in his left hand; in his right he holds up a small wooden crucifix, the Christ on it with head gently bowed toward him, recalling the crucifix of San Miniato. Behind him, the shady valley of Vallombrosa in the Tuscan Apennines: tall dark firs, a small stone monastery with a bell-cote, a stream, and far below the Arno valley toward Florence in blue haze. Humble, forgiving and serene; no lettering.
cards.face: A Florentine of about seventy, lean from austerity, with a fair, lightly weathered complexion and a face BROADEST ACROSS HIGH, JUTTING CHEEKBONES, the cheeks falling FLAT beneath them to a NARROW, SQUARE-TIPPED chin; a medium straight nose with a slightly BULBOUS tip, WIDE-SET, pale grey eyes under sparse, ARCHED grey brows, a small, firm mouth under a pronounced upper-lip groove; a short, close, silver-grey beard following the jaw, grey hair in a monastic crown; the gaze lowered to the crucifix, gentle.
cards.basis: No portrait from life survives. Neri di Bicci (Santa Trinita) and Luca di Tommè paint him old, in a grey-brown habit, with a short grey beard and a monastic crown; Wikipedia gives c. 985 – 1073 and the bowing crucifix of San Miniato. The card follows the old painters, with the cheekbones and chin as our choice.

sources.title: Wikipedia, John Gualbert (lead: Neri di Bicci, Santa Trinita)
Wikipedia (it), Giovanni Gualberto (lead: Luca di Tommè)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-12-john-gualbert (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: Water quencheth a flaming fire, and alms resisteth sin.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: A água apaga o fogo abrasador, e a esmola resiste ao pecado.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-13-eugenius.md Reflection, second sentence of the quotation (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Eugenius, Bishop of Carthage, half-length, as a fifth-century African bishop without a mitre: a white tunic under a full, bell-shaped paenula of deep wine-red, a white wool pallium with small dark crosses, a plain wooden staff in the crook of his left arm; with his right hand he gives a round loaf of bread to an unseen poor man at the edge of the window (only the reaching hand shows). Behind him, Carthage by the sea: the round naval harbour, white-walled houses and a colonnaded basilica on the Byrsa hill, date palms, the blue gulf with the mountains of Cape Bon beyond. Generous, steadfast and kind; no lettering.
cards.face: A Carthaginian of Roman Africa of about sixty-five, with a warm olive-brown complexion and a LONG face with DEEPLY SUNKEN TEMPLES and a TALL, ROUNDED crown; a strongly ARCHED, bony nose, LARGE, gentle dark eyes under HEAVY LIDS, thick, curved black-grey brows, full lips in a WIDE, generous mouth, a short, TIGHTLY CURLED white beard close along the jaw, close-cropped curly white hair; the gaze turned kindly toward the poor man.
cards.basis: No likeness survives; the Milanese statue on his Wikipedia page is a generic mitred bishop. The book tells a citizen of Carthage chosen bishop in 481, charitable to excess, twice exiled by the Vandal kings, who died near Albi in 505. The card shows the alms of his Reflection; the face is ours.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Eugenius of Carthage
Wikipedia (fr), Eugène de Carthage
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-13-eugenius (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: To enjoy the privileges of the scapular, it is sufficient that it be received lawfully and worn devoutly.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Para gozar dos privilégios do escapulário, basta que seja recebido legitimamente e usado com devoção.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-16-simon-stock.md Reflection, first sentence (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Simon Stock, half-length, in the Carmelite habit: a brown tunic and brown scapular, a white mantle over the shoulders, the hood fallen back. He holds out in both hands, as if showing it, a brown scapular of two small plain rectangles of brown wool joined by cords (no lettering, no emblem), his eyes lifted toward a soft golden light at the upper corner of the window (no figure in it). Behind him, a thirteenth-century English friary of grey stone with a small chapel and cloister, beside a quiet river among willows and green fields, under a pale summer sky. Humble, grateful and full of trust; no lettering.
cards.face: St. Simon Stock as on `mount_carmel`: an Englishman of about seventy, clean-shaven, with a gaunt TRIANGULAR face — broad temples narrowing to a small pointed chin, hollow cheeks, a long, thin, slightly aquiline nose, deep-set pale blue eyes lifted in wonder under sparse white brows, a thin-lipped mouth slightly open; white hair in a narrow ring around a wide tonsure.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. The face is the one the batch-16 card `mount_carmel` already gives him, so that he looks the same on both cards. The book tells the Kentish hermit, prior general from 1245, the scapular vision at Cambridge in 1251 and his death at Bordeaux in 1265.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Simon Stock (lead: Pietro Novelli, Our Lady of Carmel and Saints)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-16-simon-stock (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: We must always be ready to sacrifice our dearest and best natural affections in obedience to the call of our heavenly Father.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Devemos estar sempre prontos a sacrificar nossas mais caras e melhores afeições naturais em obediência ao chamado de nosso Pai celestial.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-17-alexius.md Reflection, first sentence (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Alexius, half-length, as a poor beggar sheltering in his father's house: a threadbare, patched tunic of undyed grey-brown wool with a rope belt and a worn dark cloak; he sits in a dim nook beneath a marble stairway of a Roman palace, a small wooden bowl and a pilgrim's staff beside him, and holds against his breast a small folded parchment (nothing legible). Through an archway beyond the stairs, the gardens and the church of the Aventine hill and the roofs of Rome in soft morning light. Poor, hidden, patient and peaceful; no lettering.
cards.face: A Roman patrician worn down by seventeen years of beggary, about fifty-five, with a pale olive complexion and a SMALL, NARROW, TALL face — LONG, FLAT cheeks, a FINE, STRAIGHT nose with a slightly squared tip, LARGE, soft brown eyes whose outer corners SLOPE DOWN, fine, straight brows, a small, soft mouth above a SMALL, RECEDING chin; dark-brown hair roughly cropped short and greying, a sparse, patchy dark beard; the gaze lowered, gentle and hidden.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. The book, following the Greek legend, tells the patrician who fled his wedding, begged at Edessa and died unknown under his father's roof; Russian icons paint him long-haired and bearded in a dark cloak. The card keeps the beggar and the palace stair; the face is ours, kept away from the long-haired hermit type.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Alexius of Rome (lead: Russian icon)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-17-alexius (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: According to the ancient Martyrologies, St. Margaret suffered at Antioch in Pisidia, in the last general persecution.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Segundo os antigos Martirológios, Santa Margarida sofreu em Antioquia da Pisídia, na última perseguição geral.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-20-margaret.md, first sentence; the chapter has no Reflection, so the card has none (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Margaret, half-length, as a young Christian girl of Pisidia: a long-sleeved tunic of pale green under a warm rust-red mantle, a narrow white veil laid back over braided hair; she holds up a small plain wooden cross in her right hand and a green martyr's palm in her left, against her shoulder. Behind her, the upland pastures of Pisidia with a few grazing sheep, low limestone hills, and the walls of Antioch on a far slope under a clear sky. Pure, fearless and gentle; no dragon, no torments, no lettering.
cards.face: A Greek girl of Asia Minor of about sixteen, with a warm, light olive complexion and a SHORT, SQUARE face — a broad, STRAIGHT jaw ending in a small SQUARE chin, WIDE, FLAT cheekbones, a SHORT, straight nose with a broad bridge, very LARGE, WIDE-SET dark eyes under STRONG, straight, nearly level dark brows, a WIDE mouth with a full lower lip; black hair in two thick braids; the gaze direct and steady.
cards.basis: No likeness survives, and the book gives almost nothing: a martyr of Antioch in Pisidia, taught by a Christian nurse, persecuted by her pagan father. The Western image of her rising from a dragon is the part even the Golden Legend called fable, so the card shows the shepherdess of her Life with a cross and palm. The square face keeps her apart from the oval virgin martyrs.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Margaret the Virgin (lead: Cretan icon)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-20-margaret (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: Victor, a Christian officer in the troops, went about in the night-time from house to house, visiting the faithful and inspiring them with contempt of a temporal death and the love of eternal life.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Vítor, um oficial cristão das tropas, ia de noite de casa em casa, visitando os fiéis e inspirando-lhes o desprezo de uma morte temporal e o amor da vida eterna.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-21-victor.md, first paragraph, the third sentence after its opening phrase "In this general consternation,"; the chapter has no Reflection, so the card has none (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Victor, half-length, as a Roman army officer of the late third century: a muscled bronze cuirass over a russet tunic, leather shoulder straps, a deep-blue military cloak pinned at the right shoulder, no helmet; he holds a green palm in his right hand, his left resting on the rim of a small round stone hand-mill millstone set upright beside him. Behind him, Marseilles: the long harbour inlet with moored Roman ships, the white limestone hills, and on the rocky slope across the water a cave-mouth among pines where the Christians buried him. Resolute, cheerful and brave; no wounds, no lettering.
cards.face: A Gallo-Roman of Massilia of about thirty-five, weathered by service, with a fair, sun-reddened complexion and a strong, ANGULAR face — a broad, straight forehead, SHARPLY CUT cheekbones, the sides running straight down to a BROAD, FLAT-BOTTOMED chin with a vertical CLEFT; a SHORT nose with a slight BREAK at the bridge; deep-set, bright blue-grey eyes under thick, LOW, straight sandy brows; a wide, thin-lipped mouth; thick, straight sandy-brown hair cut short, a short, close sandy beard; the gaze frank and steady.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. The book tells the officer at Marseilles under Maximian, the converted guards, the kicked altar and the millstone; the Dutch and Belgian images on Wikipedia show a bearded soldier with a millstone, his traditional attribute. The fair, broken-nosed soldier's face is ours.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Victor of Marseilles
Wikipedia (fr), Victor de Marseille (lead: statue with millstone)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-21-victor (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: Christina remained unshaken in her faith.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Cristina permaneceu inabalável em sua fé.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-24-christina.md, first paragraph, last sentence; the chapter has no Reflection, so the card has none (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Christina, half-length, as a young girl of a rich Roman family: a long white tunic, a sky-blue mantle edged in gold, a thin gold circlet in her hair; she holds a green palm and two plain arrows crossed in her right hand, her left hand on her breast; a small round millstone rests at her side. Behind her, the lake of Bolsena: calm blue water with its two small wooded islands, the town of Bolsena with its castle on the hill, olive groves and vineyards on the green shore. Innocent, calm and unafraid; no wounds, no torments, no lettering.
cards.face: An Etruscan-Roman girl of about thirteen, visibly a young girl, with a fair, rosy complexion and a face like a small INVERTED TRIANGLE — a HIGH, ROUNDED, PROMINENT forehead over a SHORT lower face and a small, POINTED chin; a tiny, UPTURNED nose; large, ROUND, light-brown eyes set FAR APART under fine, pale, high-arched brows; a small, bow-shaped mouth; wavy fair-auburn hair falling to the shoulders; the gaze lifted, candid and serene.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. The book tells the magistrate's daughter who broke her father's golden idols, was thrown into the lake of Bolsena with a stone and died by arrows; Wikipedia records her tomb and cult at Bolsena by the fourth century and the millstone and arrows as her attributes (Lotto's altarpiece, the Ravensburg statue). The face is ours, a young girl kept apart from the oval virgin martyrs.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Christina of Bolsena (lead: Ravensburg statue)
Wikipedia (it), Cristina di Bolsena (lead: Lorenzo Lotto)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-24-christina (chapter and engraving, public domain)

prayerExcerpt.en-US: With the elect thou shalt be elect, and with the perverse wilt be perverted.
prayerExcerpt.pt-BR: Com os eleitos serás eleito, e com os perversos serás pervertido.

cards.excerptSource: content/books/pictorial-lives-of-saints/{en-US,pt-BR}/jul-27-pantaleon.md Reflection, the whole of it (Pictorial Lives, public domain)
cards.subject: St. Pantaleon, half-length, as a young Greek physician of Nicomedia: a white chiton with narrow purple bands and a rose-red chlamys pinned at the right shoulder; he holds a small open wooden box of medicines against his side with his left hand and a slender long-handled silver spoon in his right, a green palm tucked into the crook of his arm. Behind him, Nicomedia on its gulf: a colonnaded street climbing the hill, a domed building, cypresses, and the blue water of the Sea of Marmara. Compassionate, grave and gentle; no lettering.
cards.face: A Bithynian Greek of about twenty-nine, BEARDLESS, with a warm olive complexion and a LONG, SMOOTH face — a HIGH, NARROW forehead under a low cap of short, TIGHT dark-brown curls, a LONG, THIN, straight nose with slightly flared nostrils, large ALMOND-SHAPED dark eyes set rather CLOSE under finely arched dark brows, smooth, lean cheeks, a SMALL, full, closed mouth, a LONG, narrow, rounded chin; the gaze direct and compassionate.
cards.basis: No likeness survives. Byzantine tradition, which Wikipedia describes and the Hosios Loukas mosaic shows, paints him as a beardless young physician with short curls, holding a medicine box and a spoon; the book tells the emperor's physician recalled by Hermolaus and beheaded at Nicomedia in 303. The card follows the tradition.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Saint Pantaleon (lead: Hosios Loukas mosaic)
Pictorial Lives of the Saints, jul-27-pantaleon (chapter and engraving, public domain)
